amendments.rule: An inflected verb may align to an English subject pronoun, auxiliary, and main verb together. Choose the lexical English verb as the target head. **This permission is specific to a pronoun realizing the verb's person and number.** A lexical English subject noun the ASV supplies where no source nominal is present answers to no morpheme and is its own `added` unit: `יָשְׁבוּ בָהּ` → *men shall dwell therein* gives *shall dwell* to the verb and leaves *men* `added`. **A volitive English frame belongs to the verb whose mood it renders.** Where the ASV expands an imperative or jussive with *Oh* or *Oh that ... would*, the framing words join the verb's unit and the unit heads on its lexical predicate: `הוֹדוּ` → *Oh give thanks* heads on *thanks* under rule 44, and `יוֹדוּ` → *Oh that ... would praise* heads on *praise*. A lexical subject noun supplied inside that frame is still `added` under the preceding sentence — *Oh that men would praise* leaves *men* outside the verb's discontinuous unit. This applies only where no optative particle or multi-source optative idiom stands in the Hebrew; a present `לוּ` or `מִי יִתֵּן` takes its own fixed English formula under rule 30. **A presentative dummy *there* is not such a lexical subject.** Where the ASV recasts a finite verb or participle with a presentative frame — `יֵּצֵא` → *there came forth*, `נִשֵּׂאת` → *there was lifted up* — the dummy belongs to the verb's unit, by the same constructional reasoning that puts it on `הָיָה` under rule 21, and the unit still heads on the lexical verb. When the verse also has an explicit subject noun, that noun's tokens are its own unit and only a genuinely pleonastic pronoun stays with the verb. **Where the ASV recasts a waw plus an explicit subject pronoun as a relative clause, the English *who* or *which* realizes the pronoun; the waw is `unrepresented` if the ASV writes no separate connective.** Do not give the relative pronoun to the waw merely because it opens the recast clause: `וְהוּא אַחֲרָיו` → *which was behind him* gives *which* to `הוּא` and leaves the waw unrepresented, and `וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי` → *who am old* gives *who* to `אֲנִי` on the same terms. **A question auxiliary the ASV fronts belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb.** English marks a yes-or-no question by fronting an auxiliary, and where `הֲ` stands in the clause that word is what the ASV has written for it: `הֲלוֹא לֶאֱמוּנָה` → *do not thine eyes look upon truth* gives *do* to `הֲ` in a clause that has no verb at all to take it, and `הַעַל אֵלֶּה לֹא אֶפְקֹד` → *Shall I not visit* gives *Shall* to `הֲ` and *I visit* to the verb, even though that auxiliary also carries the imperfect's future. The `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question is read the same way, since it is what marks that clause as the second question: `אִם לֹא תָחִילוּ` → *will ye not tremble* gives *will* to `אִם` and *ye tremble* to the verb. **But a particle for which the ASV has written a connective of its own is not a home for the auxiliary as well.** Where the ASV renders that `אִם`, or another particle standing at the head of the second question, by a written *Or*, *Or if* or another connective, that word is the particle's under rule 14, the particle takes no second English word, and the fronted auxiliary is the ordinary one this rule's first sentence gives the verb: `אִם יְדַבֵּר אֵלֶיךָ רַכּוֹת` → ***Or*** *will he speak soft words unto thee* gives *Or* to `אִם` and *will he speak* to the verb. This is the reasoning of this rule's second limit below, where an interrogative holding an English word of its own leaves the auxiliary to the verb, and of rule 51's ruling that a waw holding a connective of its own is not a home for a second word. Count the clause's English function words against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s; where the ASV writes no connective for the particle, the preceding sentence governs as before. Where the ASV marks the question by inversion alone and writes no auxiliary, the particle is `unrepresented`: `הַאוֹתִי לֹא תִירָאוּ` → *Fear ye not me*. Two limits. Where no interrogative morpheme is present at all, a fronted *do* is the verb's own under this rule's first sentence: `לֹא שָׁפָטוּ` → *do they not judge*. And this governs the yes-or-no particle only: an interrogative word that has an English word of its own — `מָה` → *what*, `אֵי` → *How* — leaves the fronted auxiliary to the verb, as `אֵי לָזֹאת אֶסְלַח לָךְ` → *How can I pardon thee* leaves *can I pardon* whole. **And a particle heading an indirect question takes the subordinating word the ASV writes for it, which puts it in that same position.** Where `הֲ` introduces a question embedded under a verb of testing, seeing, knowing or asking and the ASV writes *whether* or *if* at the head of the embedded clause, that word is what the particle is rendered by: the particle takes it and heads on it, and a modal or auxiliary the ASV fronts inside that clause belongs to the predicate under this rule's first sentence. `לְמַעַן נַסּוֹת בָּם אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל הֲשֹׁמְרִים הֵם אֶת־דֶּרֶךְ יְהוָה` → *that I may prove Israel,* ***whether*** *they* ***will keep*** *the way of Jehovah* gives *whether* to `הֲ` and *will keep* to the participial predicate, while the explicit pronoun keeps only its own *they* under rule 20. This is the count the paragraph above runs, read for the first question rather than the second: a particle already holding an English word of its own is not a home for a second one, as rule 51 says of a waw, and giving it both would leave the predicate's auxiliary unaccounted against rule 2. The corpus aligns an interrogative `הַ` to *whether* in six units. Read what the ASV has written before reaching for this sentence: where it marks the embedded question by the fronted auxiliary alone and writes no subordinator, the particle takes that auxiliary as in a direct question, and where it writes neither, the particle is `unrepresented` as above. **An English matrix duration frame is not an auxiliary of the finite verb inside the temporal clause it introduces.** Where `עַד` plus a temporal interrogative and `לֹא` plus a finite verb is rendered *how long will it be ere ...*, the temporal-interrogative expression takes *how long will it be* as one `noncompositional` unit, headed on *long*; the negative takes *ere*; and the finite verb takes only its subordinate subject and predicate. `עַד מָתַי לֹא יוּכְלוּ` → *how long will it be ere they attain* and `עַד אָנָה לֹא תִשְׁקֹטִי` → *how long will it be ere thou be quiet* follow that division. The dummy *it* is not the finite verb's person and number, and assigning the matrix frame to that verb would give it two English clauses. This does not make a simple *how long ...* indivisible where the ASV writes no separate matrix frame; there each morpheme is aligned on its own merits under rule 2. **Where the ASV recasts a waw plus a finite verb as a relative clause and no explicit subject pronoun stands in that clause, the relative *who* or *which* is the connective the ASV has written for the waw and belongs to the waw; the verb keeps its subject, auxiliaries and lexical verb.** `וַתֹּאכַל` → *which hath devoured* gives *which* to the waw and *hath devoured* to the verb. This is the other side of the explicit-pronoun case above: a present pronoun takes the relative before the waw does, but without one the waw is the morpheme licensing the relative connective. Where no waw or other conjunction stands either, rule 55 governs the supplied relative instead. The finished corpus aligns a waw directly to *which* in ten units, so this is settled rather than a tie to hedge.
amendments.why: Rule 17's second limit as written scopes the 'interrogative holding an English word of its own leaves the auxiliary to the verb' reasoning to interrogative words such as mah and ey, and expressly excludes the yes-or-no particle from it ('this governs the yes-or-no particle only'). JDG.2.22 is the case the rule had not considered: ha heads an indirect question under a verb of testing, the ASV writes 'whether' for it and fronts 'will' before the participial predicate. Read literally, the earlier sentence would give 'will' to ha as well and leave 'whether' with no morpheme, against rule 2, while the rule's own counting sentence and its Or-if paragraph point the other way. The amendment widens that paragraph's reasoning to a particle heading the first question rather than the second, which is where the chapter met it. Corpus supports rather than contradicts: LEMMA=ha shows six units aligned to 'whether', including ECC.3.21 twice, and none aligning an indirect-question particle to a fronted modal beside a written 'whether'. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule so the over-broad limit is corrected where a later pass will read it.

conventions: Where a verb whose own lexeme carries a direction stands before min and the ASV writes both a directional particle and an ablative preposition, the particle answering to that verb's direction is the verb's and min takes what remains. JDG.2.1 gives 'up' to the hiphil of alah and 'out of' to min (I made you to go up out of Egypt); JDG.2.12 gives 'out' to the hiphil of yatsa and 'of' to min (who brought them out of the land of Egypt); JDG.2.15 gives 'out' to yatsa qal inside 'they went out'. Where no such verb stands, min takes 'out of' whole, headed on 'out' (2.16, 2.17, 2.18). The competing reading at 2.12, which gives 'out of' whole to min and leaves a bare 'brought' for the causative verb, is recorded in that verse's notes under rule 8.

report: Checked all 54 candidate lemmas, plus an end-to-end read of the dump for the asymmetry the lemma table is blind to: a supplied English word marked `added` in one verse and folded into a licensing morpheme in another. The chapter's three `added` units (2.3 'as thorns', 2.17 'but', 2.22 'it') each answer to no morpheme standing in their own clause, and nowhere else does the chapter fold a word of that kind into a neighbour. No construction is analysed two ways without something in the source or in the ASV licensing the difference; verdict no-change, patches empty.

Waw: every treatment is a connective the ASV actually wrote (And, and, that, nor, but, then, So, when, Wherefore, so that, Now when, who), read off the ASV as rule 14's open list directs. The one unrepresented waw (2.6, apodosis) follows from the preceding waw taking 'Now when' whole under rule 55. Waw plus a negative fuses to 'neither' only at 2.23, where one English word carries both senses, and splits at 2.2, 2.14 and 2.20 where the ASV writes two; 2.10 and 2.19 give a bare waw 'nor' with the negation written elsewhere or gapped. All three shapes are rule 35 applied to what is written.

Article: 'the' wherever the ASV writes one before the article's own word, unrepresented wherever a demonstrative or possessive holds the phrase's single determiner (2.2, 2.4, 2.5, 2.10, 2.19, 2.20, 2.23). Rules 29, 41 and 47 are applied identically each time, including the two bracketed assimilated tokens at 2.13, which are aligned separately and correctly. Every unrepresented preposition is a rule 40 or 52 recasting for which the ASV writes no function word at all.

Preposition plus construct noun: split at 2.3 and 2.21 ('from before', a word for each morpheme), fused at 2.18 ('by reason of') and 2.14 ('before', headed on the construct noun). That is rule 30's one-rendering condition read as that rule states it, with 'from before' as its own named counterexample. halak-ahare fuses to 'followed'/'following' at 2.12 and 2.19 and splits at 2.17 where the ASV writes 'after' separately.

The one candidate worth naming: min takes a bare 'of' at 2.12 ('brought them out of the land') but 'out of' at 2.1, 2.16, 2.17 and 2.18. This is licensed rather than a split. The chapter gives the directional particle to whichever verb's own lexeme writes that direction and lets min take the remainder, so the hiphil of yatsa takes 'out' and min takes 'of', while at 2.1 the hiphil of alah takes 'up' and min takes 'out of'. The same principle runs at 2.15 ('went out'). Recorded as a convention; 2.12's note already names the competing reading, which would give 'out of' whole to min and leave 'brought' alone for the verb. That is the chapter's one edge a targeted corpus query on the exodus formula could still move, and it was left as the verse pass took it because the chapter applies one principle to both verses.
